name: S3 bucket with public-read ACL
explanation: The vulnerable version sets the bucket ACL to public-read, exposing every object in the bucket to anyone with the URL. The patched version removes the explicit ACL (defaulting to private) and attaches a public_access_block resource that explicitly denies any future attempt to grant public access. The four block flags should always be true for non-static-website buckets; setting them belt-and-braces protects against misconfigurations introduced later via console / IAM.

name: IAM trust policy with wildcard Principal
explanation: The vulnerable trust policy lets any AWS account in the world assume the role - the wildcard Principal is a complete trust boundary failure. The patched version pins the trust to a specific account ARN and adds an ExternalId condition so even if someone discovers the role ARN, they need the shared secret to assume it. ExternalId is the canonical defence against the 'confused deputy' problem in cross-account IAM.

name: Security group with 0.0.0.0/0 ingress on management port
explanation: The vulnerable version exposes SSH (port 22) to the entire internet. The patched version restricts the ingress source to a variable list of corporate / VPN CIDRs. The same fix applies to RDP (3389), database ports (3306, 5432, 1433, 27017), and management interfaces (Kubernetes API 6443, Docker 2375/2376). The hard rule: management ports never get 0.0.0.0/0.

name: Pod running as root with privileged: true
vulnerable:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: app:1.0
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
      runAsUser: 0
patched:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    fsGroup: 10001
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: app:1.0
    securityContext:
      privileged: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop:
          - ALL
explanation: The vulnerable pod runs as root inside a privileged container, which means a container escape compromises the host. The patched version sets runAsNonRoot at the pod level, drops all Linux capabilities, sets the root filesystem read-only, and forbids privilege escalation. Together these reduce the blast radius of a code-execution exploit inside the container to near-zero impact on the node.

name: No NetworkPolicy in namespace (default-allow)
vulnerable:
# (No NetworkPolicy resources in the namespace)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: app-prod
patched:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: app-prod
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: app-prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
explanation: Kubernetes namespaces default to allow-all pod-to-pod traffic, so a compromised pod in any namespace can talk to every other pod cluster-wide. The patched version adds a default-deny NetworkPolicy that selects every pod in the namespace and forbids all ingress/egress; specific allow policies are then added on top. This is the namespace-level equivalent of a stateful-firewall default-deny rule.

name: RDS without encryption-at-rest
patched:
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  identifier         = "prod-db"
  engine             = "postgres"
  storage_encrypted  = true
  kms_key_id         = aws_kms_key.rds.arn
  deletion_protection = true
  backup_retention_period = 30
}
explanation: The vulnerable RDS has unencrypted storage, so a snapshot leak or volume access on the underlying EBS exposes the entire database. The patched version uses customer-managed KMS encryption (giving you the audit trail + revocation capability), enables deletion_protection (prevents accidental destroy), and extends backup_retention to 30 days. The KMS-key-via-CMK pattern is preferred over default AWS-managed keys because it gives you per-key access control and key rotation policy.

name: IAM policy with action wildcard *:*
explanation: The vulnerable policy grants every action on every resource - effectively root in AWS. The patched version restricts to specific actions on a specific bucket prefix. The least-privilege principle for IAM: each policy should name the actions it needs (no wildcards), the resources it acts on (no Resource: *), and where applicable conditions that further bound the access (e.g. aws:SourceVpc). When the policy can't be authored that tightly, attach a permissions boundary that caps what the policy can ever grant.

name: Secret stored in plaintext in manifest
vulnerable:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
stringData:
  password: "sup3rs3cret!"
patched:
# Secret materialised from external secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager,
# Vault, GCP Secret Manager) via External Secrets Operator.
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: db-creds
  data:
  - secretKey: password
    remoteRef:
      key: prod/db/password
explanation: The vulnerable manifest has the password in cleartext, so it ends up in git history (assuming the manifest is in source control), in CI logs, in any tooling that reads the manifest, and in `kubectl get secret -o yaml` output for anyone with read access. The patched version uses External Secrets Operator to materialise the secret from a real secret store at runtime; the manifest in git only contains the reference, not the value. Rotating the secret is then 'update the value in Secrets Manager,' not 'rebase your git history.'

name: S3 bucket without access logging
explanation: The vulnerable bucket has no access logging, so when an incident happens you have no audit trail of who read or wrote which object. The patched version writes server access logs to a separate logs bucket (separate so a compromise of the data bucket doesn't take the audit trail with it) and enables object versioning so deleted objects can be restored from before the incident. Both are operationally cheap and forensically essential.

name: CloudFront distribution without HTTPS
explanation: The vulnerable CloudFront distribution accepts plain HTTP, so users on hostile networks (coffee shops, mobile carriers in some regions) get man-in-the-middled. The patched version forces HTTPS via a 301 redirect, attaches an ACM certificate, and pins the minimum TLS version to 1.2 (TLS 1.0 / 1.1 are deprecated; TLS 1.3 is the long-term goal but 1.2 has the broadest client support today). Always pair with HSTS at the application layer.

name: ClusterRoleBinding granting cluster-admin to default ServiceAccount
vulnerable:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: app-admin
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: default
  namespace: app-prod
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
patched:
# Use a dedicated ServiceAccount, not 'default', and bind only the
# specific verbs/resources the workload actually needs.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-svc
  namespace: app-prod
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role  # Role, not ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: app-prod-svc
  namespace: app-prod
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: app-svc-binding
  namespace: app-prod
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: app-svc
  namespace: app-prod
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: app-prod-svc
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
explanation: Granting cluster-admin to the default SA in any namespace means every pod in that namespace runs as cluster-admin (because pods that don't specify a serviceAccountName get the default). The patched version creates a named SA, a Role (namespaced, not ClusterRole) with only the specific verbs needed, and a RoleBinding. The least-privilege RBAC pattern: never bind to default, never use cluster-admin for workloads, prefer Role over ClusterRole when scope allows.

name: EBS volume without encryption
explanation: The vulnerable volume has unencrypted storage. Snapshot leaks or compromise of the AWS account expose the data. The patched version uses customer-managed KMS encryption AND sets account-wide encryption-by-default so any future EBS volume gets encrypted automatically, even if Terraform code somewhere forgets. Combine with snapshot-policy that encrypts cross-region copies.

name: Pod with hostNetwork: true exposing host network namespace
vulnerable:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  hostPID: true
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: app:1.0
patched:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  hostNetwork: false
  hostPID: false
  hostIPC: false
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: app:1.0
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
      name: http
explanation: hostNetwork: true puts the pod in the host's network namespace - the pod can sniff every other pod's traffic on the node, bind to host ports, and reach kubelet. hostPID: true lets it see and signal every host process. The patched version turns these off and uses a container port bound through service-level load balancing, which is the kubernetes-native way to expose pod traffic. hostNetwork should only be used for special infra workloads (CNI plugins, ingress controllers) where the network-namespace sharing is genuinely required.

name: IAM user without MFA enforced for console access
explanation: The vulnerable IAM user has console access without any MFA enforcement, so a stolen password is full account access. The patched version forces MFA via a deny-when-MFA-absent policy attached to the user, and adds a strict account-wide password policy. The 'BoolIfExists' / 'false' pattern is the canonical way to require MFA - it denies the action if MFA isn't present (and treats absence of the MFA context as 'no').

name: ALB without WAF attached
vulnerable:
resource "aws_lb" "web" {
  name               = "web-alb"
  internal           = false
  load_balancer_type = "application"
  security_groups    = [aws_security_group.web.id]
  subnets            = aws_subnet.public.*.id
}
explanation: The vulnerable ALB has no WAF in front of it, so common L7 attacks (SQLi, XSS, path traversal, request smuggling) hit the application directly. The patched version attaches a WAFv2 ACL with the AWS-managed CommonRuleSet (which covers the OWASP Top 10 patterns) plus turns on drop_invalid_header_fields at the ALB itself (which silently drops malformed headers that some smuggling attacks rely on). The CloudWatch metrics give you visibility into what the WAF is blocking.
